leads.work: Weekly 'California Capacity Report' that Michelle Lokay writes by hand. Each Friday (or Thursday) she pulls TW and El Paso average deliveries to California, capacity utilization by delivery point, and the Gas Daily prices with their changes, then emails the same fixed-format summary to the same 7 recipients.
leads.why: Six or more weeks in a row of identical-template emails with only the numbers changed. The figures come from systems and published indices, so the report is a strong candidate for automatic generation.

leads.work: Daily Energy Market Report (Economic Insight) that Jill Chatterton forwards by hand to the Portland trading group.
leads.why: An admin re-sends the full report to a fixed list of about 12 traders every day. A direct subscription or list routing would remove the step.

leads.work: Manual reconciliation of OBA and interconnect imbalances with Mojave and CIG (El Paso). Volumes are compared month by month back to 1996–98, daily volume statements are faxed back and forth, Location Quantity Summary printouts are requested, and discrepancies are summarized one by one. The work ends in cash-out and payback settlement.
leads.why: Labor-intensive back-and-forth over weeks: faxes, re-sent spreadsheets, a separate request to a colleague for printouts. Discrepancies going back years point to no routine automated tie-out between pipelines, and the related imbalance and line-pack summaries recur.

leads.work: Meter volume recaps in 'the usual format', tied out against scheduled quantities, with exceptions worked through with the operator.
leads.why: 'Usual format' points to a regular manual recap. Comparing scheduled and measured volumes is rule-based and can be automated.

leads.work: Monthly Mojave/El Paso Topock index price lookups done by hand for billing or settlement, including re-sending after a price was revised.
leads.why: A colleague asks by email for four months of index prices, then a revised February price and the March price follow in further emails. A direct feed of index data to billing would remove the hand-off.

leads.work: Biweekly time-report reminders from the admin (Audrey Robertson), with each person replying by email with their sick and vacation days.
leads.why: The same 'Time Reports Due' blast recurs every pay period, followed by manual absence replies and corrections ('you were here yesterday'). A self-service timekeeping system could replace the loop.

leads.work: Weekly 'bullets' status collection by Kimberly Watson from each marketer, who must reply even when they have nothing to report.
leads.why: A recurring manual roll-up of status updates by email, with each reply forwarded on again.

leads.work: TW contract administration by email: a contract status list (processing, tendered, executed), amendment requests, name changes, MAXDTQ changes, and the routing of executed agreements.
leads.why: The status report looks like a recurring manual snapshot. Each change goes through several emails between the customer, the marketer and Contract Administration, such as a customer having to 'email officially' for a name change.

leads.work: Billing TCR surcharges on expired contracts by manually overriding the CBS billing system or drafting amendments.
leads.why: A system gap: the surcharge runs for 10 years after a contract expires, but CBS cannot bill expired contracts, so each case needs manual workarounds and coordination.

leads.work: TW Unsubscribed Capacity web posting: formatting problems, and postings going up late so that shippers call before they are live.
leads.why: A 'long-standing issue' with headers and printing, reworked several times. A note says the posting 'went up late again', which suggests a recurring manual posting process that should be automated or scheduled.

leads.work: UBS migration compliance: each employee copies their own H/O/M drive data and email (exporting from Outlook loses attachments), signs the data migration certification, and has forms collected in batches by admins.
leads.why: Every one of hundreds of employees did this by hand under deadline, with repeat clarifications ('may not have been clear'), forms gathered by Cara Semperger, and broken export instructions. It is costly, and the same pattern applies to any future transfer of staff to a new entity.

leads.work: Per-user access provisioning: production IDs and passwords emailed one by one (in plain text), TDS book access granted through a hand-distributed application, Sitara URL changes passed along by email, and new folder permissions.
leads.why: Several separate emails for each user and system. Credentials in plain-text email is also a risk. Provisioning could be centralized.

leads.work: Requests to keep EST (estate) accounts open past the cutoff, plus hand-over of procedures still run by UBS staff to the estate team.
leads.why: A long reply chain to work out who needs exceptions. Each user has to email the reason and duration, and someone asks for a list of procedures still running. No inventory of who runs which process appears to exist.

leads.work: Daily real-time and scheduling work: EPE (El Paso Electric) schedules and models saved to set paths and sent to Kathy, and daily CAPS settlement (DA/HA finals).
leads.why: Daily file-based steps that broke during the migration. Moving files to fixed paths and emailing models are candidates for automation.

leads.work: Individual pre-employment compliance chasers (drug tests) and orientation, benefits-form and access-card logistics.
leads.why: HR sends the same email to each person one at a time and tracks completion by hand, with repeated reminders and RSVP-by-reply. A tracking checklist or workflow would fit better.

leads.work: Testing for trading platform launch: a simulation, test deals pushed through Tagg/Sitara that must be checked by hand for booking and valuation, and product setup in Stack Manager.
leads.why: Manual verification of deals across systems, coordinated by email. Repeatable test scripts could reduce the effort.

leads.work: Expense report approval notices from Concur for small amounts (for example $30), entered by an admin for the employee.
leads.why: Every small claim goes through an admin, then an approval. Worth checking volume across the archive and whether low-value claims could be auto-approved.

leads.work: Meeting and training scheduling done by email back-and-forth: project meetings, CAS training slots, strategy meetings, cancellations, and interview scheduling for the trading assistant role.
leads.why: Several messages per meeting just to settle a time. Shared calendars or booking tools would cut this.

leads.work: CAISO market notices (HA republish, transmission derates, procedure updates, settlement files, OMAR simulation, MD02 documents, TSWG calls) that must be passed on to operating departments.
leads.why: A high volume of automated notices that the recipient is asked to forward by hand, and some are re-sent with corrected attachments. Routing or filtering rules could handle them.

leads.work: Facility cost estimates (Level A/B) for interconnect and lateral projects, built in spreadsheets and passed between Facility Planning and marketing, with requests for summary economics.
leads.why: Estimates are built by hand for each project, and executives have to chase for the economics. Standard templates or models may help.

leads.work: Admin information requests and surveys: club membership reimbursement details, distribution-list adds, office move labels, the on-call schedule, and toner notices.
leads.why: Small recurring admin requests handled through manual email collection. Self-service forms could absorb them.

leads.work: Retiring unused applications (TW Deal Profitability and TW Deal Analysis), which are still being supported with no users.
leads.why: IT is paying to support apps nobody uses and has to ask users by voicemail and email. A usage inventory could find more of these.

leads.work: Heavy personal use of work email (jokes, eBay links, job searches, personal forwards).
leads.why: Many non-business forwards from one mailbox. Low priority, but it shows time spent and storage used.
